column1: Before powering on, scan for loose tubes, cables, and connectors.
A clean sensor is a reliable sensor—wipe it before trusting the reading.
If a value looks “too perfect,” verify with a second measurement.
Treat alarms as information, not noise—identify the cause before silencing.
Confirm the device mode matches the clinical goal, not just the last setting used.
Check the patient interface first: mask seal, tubing kinks, and fit solve many “device problems.”
When changing settings, adjust one parameter at a time to track cause and effect.
Trend beats snapshot: compare values over minutes, not seconds.
If the waveform looks wrong, inspect the line—occlusions and leaks distort everything.
A quick pre-use checklist prevents a long troubleshooting session later.
Label lines and ports; confusion loves unlabeled connections.
Use the “pause and point” habit: point to the parameter you’re changing, then confirm out loud.
Low battery warnings are a countdown—plan your next steps immediately.
Calibrate when recommended; “close enough” drifts over time.
Verify disposables match the correct type and size before assembly.
A small leak can mimic a big problem—listen, feel, and inspect seals.
Avoid overtightening connectors; damaged threads create recurring leaks.
If you swap a component, re-check the full system path from source to patient.
Make room for airflow: blocked vents lead to heat issues and unstable performance.
Keep the cable path tidy—strain relief reduces disconnections mid-procedure.
Don’t chase a single number; cross-check with the patient’s clinical signs.
Set alarm limits intentionally; default thresholds are not “one size fits all.”
Use priority thinking: address life-critical alarms before comfort alarms.
When a sensor reads flatline, suspect contact first, failure second.
If the monitor shows artifacts, reduce motion and check electrode/clip placement.
A zero reading can mean “not connected,” not “no signal.”
Switching patients? Reset profiles and clear old trends to avoid confusion.
Confirm time and date settings—bad timestamps ruin traceability.
Document configuration changes; future you will thank present you.
Backups matter: know where the manual method is before you need it.
Use a consistent setup order every time; routines reduce mistakes.
When in doubt, return to a known-safe baseline configuration.
Take a photo of the setup (if your protocol allows) to speed up audits and troubleshooting.
Keep spare consumables within reach—running out creates risky improvisation.
If a filter looks saturated, replace it; performance drops silently.
Verify the gas/liquid source status before blaming the device.
Check for occlusions by following the line with your hand from end to end.
Use “two-step confirmation” for critical actions: select, then verify, then apply.
Avoid rapid toggling; give the system time to stabilize after changes.
Confirm the correct patient weight/parameters—many calculations depend on them.
Keep connectors dry; moisture causes false signals and intermittent errors.
Use only approved cleaning methods; harsh chemicals degrade seals and plastics.
If you hear an unusual sound, pause—mechanical clues often come before alarms.
Don’t silence recurring alarms without solving the root cause—recurrence is a warning pattern.
Review the last event log when something feels “off”; the sequence tells the story.
A stable baseline reading after setup is your green light to proceed.
Make sure the device is on a stable surface; vibration can affect precision.
Confirm the right ports: “fits” doesn’t mean “correct.”
Plan your disconnection steps—avoid accidental air entry or contamination.
End each session with a quick post-check: clean, inspect, restock, and log issues.
